On the Slow Convergence of Impatient Methods
    A. Researcher and B. Coauthor
    March 3, 2025
============================================

Abstract

    We revisit the classical fixed-point iteration and show that impatience
    costs precisely one order of convergence. The argument is elementary[1]
    and the constants are explicit.

1 Introduction
--------------

Fixed-point iteration is the oldest trick in numerical analysis <cit.>. Given
a contraction 𝑇 on a complete metric space, the sequence 𝑥ₙ₊₁ = 𝑇(𝑥ₙ)
converges to the unique fixed point 𝑥^⋆, and the rate is governed by the
Lipschitz constant 𝐿 < 1:

    𝑑(𝑥ₙ, 𝑥^⋆ ) ≤ (𝐿ⁿ)/(1 - 𝐿) 𝑑(𝑥₁, 𝑥₀).

What we add to this picture is the observation that 𝑠𝑡𝑜𝑝𝑝𝑖𝑛𝑔 𝑒𝑎𝑟𝑙𝑦 — the
practice we call 𝐢𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 — changes the exponent rather than the constant.

2 Setting
---------

Throughout, (𝑋, 𝑑) is a complete metric space and 𝑇 : 𝑋 → 𝑋 satisfies 𝑑(𝑇(𝑥),
𝑇(𝑦)) ≤ 𝐿 𝑑(𝑥, 𝑦) for all 𝑥, 𝑦 ∈ 𝑋. We assume:
  • 0 < 𝐿 < 1, so that 𝑇 is a genuine contraction;
  • 𝑥₀ ∈ 𝑋 is arbitrary, and α = 𝑑(𝑥₁, 𝑥₀) > 0;
  • the tolerance ε satisfies ε < α.

The three assumptions are independent, and each is used exactly once below.

2.1 The impatient stopping rule
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

An 𝑖𝑚𝑝𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑒𝑛𝑡 run stops at the first index 𝑛 with 𝑑(𝑥ₙ₊₁, 𝑥ₙ) ≤ ε, rather than
at the first 𝑛 with 𝑑(𝑥ₙ, 𝑥^⋆ ) ≤ ε. The two differ by a factor of 1 - 𝐿,
which is small exactly when the iteration is slow.

Theorem. Let 𝑛^⋆ be the impatient stopping index. Then 𝑑( 𝑥_𝑛^⋆ , 𝑥^⋆ ) ≤ ε/(1
- 𝐿), and this bound is attained.

Proof. Sum the geometric series ∑_(𝑘 ≥ 0) 𝐿ᵏ from the triangle inequality, and
note that equality holds for the affine map 𝑇(𝑥) = 𝐿𝑥 on ℝ. □

3 Experiments
-------------

We ran the iteration for four values of 𝐿. The measured iteration counts are:

---------------------------------
Contraction 𝐿  Patient  Impatient
---------------------------------
0.5                 34         33
0.9                219        197
0.99              2291       1832
---------------------------------

Table: Iterations to reach ε = 10⁻⁶.

The gap widens as 𝐿 → 1, as Theorem <ref> predicts.

    < g r a p h i c s >

Figure: Distance to the fixed point against the iteration count, on a
logarithmic scale.

4 Conclusion
------------

Impatience is cheap when 𝐿 is small and expensive when it is not; a
practitioner who wants the bound of Equation (<ref>) should divide the
tolerance by 1 - 𝐿 before starting.[2]

---
[1] It is elementary in the sense that it uses no machinery the reader does
    not already have.
[2] Or, equivalently, be patient.
